interest: For diplomatic and modern Japanese historians, this collection provides an extraordinary, real-time chronicle of Japan's descent into military authoritarianism and diplomatic isolation during the mid-1930s as witnessed by seasoned American observers. It is particularly valuable for its meticulous month-by-month tracking of factional violence within the Imperial Japanese Army, offering contemporaneous accounts of the Nagata assassination, the Aizawa court-martial, and the climactic February 26 Incident alongside immediate assessments of their political fallout. Furthermore, the juxtaposition of the Embassy’s detailed field despatches with internal Division of Far Eastern Affairs memoranda provides scholars with unique institutional insight into how American policymakers interpreted the convergence of Japanese constitutional crises, naval treaty abrogation, and economic nationalism before the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War.
overview: This file comprises the first part of U.S. State Department decimal file 894.00 (Political Affairs, Japan), spanning from July 1934 through March 1936 and consisting of 701 pages across 48 documents. The collection consists primarily of regular, exhaustive monthly political and economic reports (Nos. 94 through 114) compiled and forwarded by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and the staff of the American Embassy in Tokyo, accompanied by transmittal despatches, transmittal schedules of telegrams and despatches, and analytical review memoranda prepared by the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs. Across this critical period, the records document Japan's domestic political disintegration and escalating militarism—tracing the installation and travails of the Okada Cabinet, intense budget struggles led by Finance Minister Korekiyo Takahashi against escalating military expenditures, the ideological purge of Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe’s constitutional 'organ theory,' internal army factional violence culminating in the assassination of Major General Tetsuzan Nagata and the February 26, 1936 military coup attempt, and the resulting formation of the Hirota Cabinet. Concurrently, the reports thoroughly monitor Japan’s foreign and imperial policies, including the abrogation of the Washington Naval Treaty, the breakdown of the London Naval Conference, military encroachment into North China, border clashes with Soviet and Outer Mongolian forces, the finalized transfer of the Chinese Eastern Railway to Manchukuo, and diplomatic disputes surrounding the Japanese Petroleum Industry Law and the Manchukuo Oil Monopoly.
